feed.title: Media, Design & Files — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: An annotated directory of links on software, AI, security and science. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Feather Icons
entry.summary: A simple, consistent open-source icon set at a single stroke weight. Unlike large libraries it offers a minimal visual language and small file size.

entry.title: Font Awesome
entry.summary: The de facto icon and logo library of the web. Unlike collecting SVGs one by one you add icons as a font/CSS class in a single line.

entry.title: GIMP
entry.summary: A full-featured image editor that is the open-source alternative to Photoshop. Unlike paid tools it is free and extensible with plugins.

entry.title: Humaaans
entry.summary: A library of human illustrations whose parts you can mix and pose. Unlike ready illustrations you assemble the figure limb by limb into an original scene.

entry.title: Iconify
entry.summary: A library unifying 100+ icon sets under one API/component. Unlike installing each set separately you pull and mix them all from one interface.

entry.title: Icons8
entry.summary: A broad asset source offering icons, illustrations, photos and music in various styles. Unlike single-type sites it gives many types in one consistent visual language.

entry.title: Lorem Picsum
entry.summary: A service returning placeholder photos at any size (the lorem ipsum of images). Unlike fixed placeholders you pass a size in the URL and get a real photo.

entry.title: ManyPixels Gallery
entry.summary: A free illustration gallery with editable colour. Similar to unDraw; it offers a larger, topic-based collection and multiple formats.

entry.title: OpenMoji
entry.summary: An openly licensed emoji library in one design language. Unlike platform emojis it gives editable SVG emojis that look the same everywhere.

entry.title: Pexels
entry.summary: A stock source offering free photos and videos together. Unlike photo-only sites it also gives royalty-free video in the same interface.

entry.title: Pixabay
entry.summary: A royalty-free bank gathering photos, illustrations, vectors and video in one place. Unlike single-type sites it returns multi-format media in one search.

entry.title: Pixlr
entry.summary: A layer-capable image editor that runs in the browser. Unlike desktop programs it lets you do quick edits with no install.

entry.title: Remix Icon
entry.summary: A consistent open-source icon set coming in both line and solid styles. Unlike mixed sets every icon exists in both styles — consistency across a UI.

entry.title: unDraw
entry.summary: An openly licensed illustration set whose colour you can change to your brand. Unlike fixed illustrations you switch the accent colour in one place and get a consistent set.

entry.title: Unsplash
entry.summary: The largest free source of high-resolution, royalty-free photographs. Unlike paid banks it is open to commercial use with no attribution required.

entry.title: Vectorizer
entry.summary: A tool converting pixel images like PNG/JPG into vectors (SVG). Unlike redrawing by hand it automatically turns an existing logo into a scalable form.

entry.title: Whimsical
entry.summary: A tool combining flowcharts, wireframes, sticky notes and mind maps on one canvas. Unlike single-purpose tools it keeps them all together in one document.

entry.title: anything_about_game
entry.summary: A vast resource list covering every side of game development — graphics, engines, audio, academic papers. Unlike Awesome-Game-Analysis’s analysis focus it looks at the build side: it gathers every branch you need to make a game from scratch, not to dissect one.

entry.title: Awesome Game Analysis
entry.summary: A community-driven collection of resources on analysing video-game technology — engine internals, graphics techniques, file formats. Unlike game-making courses it looks the other way: not how to build, but working out what is inside shipped games.

entry.title: RetroReversing
entry.summary: A site of resources, tutorials and tools for reverse-engineering retro games — source leaks, hardware, decompilation. Unlike general reverse-engineering sites it centres on retro game hardware: it goes into console internals and period toolchains.

entry.title: 3Dassets.one
entry.summary: A search engine that consolidates several 3D asset sites into one query, filterable by licence and price. Against visiting each site, the licence filter is the point — you can isolate what is actually usable commercially.

entry.title: ambientCG
entry.summary: An archive of CC0-licensed PBR textures and materials, shipping colour, normal, roughness and displacement maps together. Unlike most texture sites the licence really is CC0 — no attribution needed, commercial use fine.

entry.title: Aseprite
entry.summary: An editor built for pixel art and animation, with onion skinning, a frame timeline and sprite sheet export. Unlike a general painting program every tool snaps to the pixel grid, so anti-aliasing never appears where you did not ask for it.

entry.title: Blender
entry.summary: Modelling, texturing, rigging, simulation, rendering and video editing in one package. Against Maya or 3ds Max it is free, and it keeps the entire pipeline in a single program so nothing is lost in file handoffs.

entry.title: CodingFont
entry.summary: Compares coding fonts two at a time in a tournament until one wins. Unlike a font list it turns browsing into a decision — it never puts twenty fonts side by side, only two.

entry.title: FontForge
entry.summary: A font creation and editing program that converts between TTF, OTF and WOFF and lets you work on glyph hinting. Unlike an online font converter, you can get at the glyphs themselves.

entry.title: Inkscape
entry.summary: A vector editor that uses SVG as its native format. Against Illustrator, the file is clean SVG ready for the web — no export step in between, and you can hand-edit the source.

entry.title: Krita
entry.summary: A painting program for digital art and concept work, with a strong brush engine and frame-by-frame animation. Unlike GIMP it was built for drawing rather than photo editing, and brush latency and stabilisation are tuned accordingly.

entry.title: LosslessCut
entry.summary: Cuts and joins video without re-encoding, working on keyframe boundaries. Against a normal editor the operation takes seconds and loses no quality — trimming the head and tail off an hour of footage no longer means opening a timeline.

entry.title: MediaInfo
entry.summary: Dumps the technical identity of a video or audio file: codec, bitrate, frame rate, colour space, container details. Unlike a player’s properties dialog it goes to stream level, which makes it the source of truth when something will not play.

entry.title: Photopea
entry.summary: An image editor in the browser that opens PSD, XCF, Sketch and XD files with their layers intact. Against GIMP it installs nothing and its PSD compatibility is genuinely good, which makes it the shortest path to opening a file someone sent you.

entry.title: Piskel
entry.summary: A pixel art and sprite animation editor in the browser. Against Aseprite it is free and needs no install; in exchange the layer and brush tools are thinner — enough for your first sprite.

entry.title: Programming Fonts
entry.summary: A place to try monospaced coding fonts side by side on real code. Unlike a font download site, you see the ligatures and the 0/O and 1/l/I distinctions in the context that actually matters.

entry.title: SankeyDiagram.net
entry.summary: Generates Sankey flow diagrams from text input, for energy, budget or funnel flows. Unlike general diagram tools it does one chart type, and takes its input as text rather than as drawing.

entry.title: ShareX
entry.summary: A screenshot and recording tool for Windows that chains post-capture steps: upload, shorten, OCR. What separates it from Snipping Tool is that workflow automation — capture and link-on-clipboard becomes one shortcut.

entry.title: Shutter Encoder
entry.summary: A converter wrapping FFmpeg with a UI, offering the intermediate codecs and batch jobs editors need. Against HandBrake it is aimed at post-production — ProRes, DNxHD and subtitle burn-in sit in the menu rather than in a command line.

entry.title: Squoosh
entry.summary: Image compression with a side-by-side comparison, running MozJPEG, WebP and AVIF encoders in the browser through WebAssembly. Unlike TinyPNG nothing is uploaded, and every encoder setting is yours to tune.

entry.title: Subtitle Edit
entry.summary: A subtitle editor that shows a waveform and spectrogram underneath, reads over 200 formats, shifts timings and extracts burned-in subtitles by OCR. Those synchronisation tools are what separate it from simple subtitle editors.

entry.title: Subtitle Editor Online
entry.summary: A subtitle editor in the browser for opening .srt and .vtt files and fixing timings and text. Against desktop tools like Subtitle Edit it installs nothing, which is what you want for a quick fix on someone else’s machine.

entry.title: The Noun Project
entry.summary: A searchable archive of millions of icons and symbols, with several visual takes on each concept. Unlike an icon library it is not a consistent set but a dictionary of concepts — the place where an icon for one very specific object actually exists.
